record.paper_title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension by virial and test transformation approaches
record.original_question: Can a thermodynamic formalism be built in which an external-field-like distortion makes an ellipsoidal deformation of a spherical vapour-liquid interface an equilibrium shape, so that the test-transformation parameter χ becomes a thermodynamic boundary condition and test-area or second-order-virial free-energy derivatives acquire a proper theoretical foundation? This would amount to introducing an additional variable—the proposed “demon” action—analogous to an external field, rather than treating the distorted ellipsoid as an ordinary equilibrium state at fixed N, V, and T.

evidence.quote: Or should we call on a demon to save us from our predicament? It might just work. Newton, the alchemist, popularized the idea of external entities intervening into bodies’ equations of motion when he argued that once planets threaten to leave their foreseen orbits, God ever so slightly pushes them back. But as we know well, one’s God is another’s demon.

The demon would distort the system in a way similar to the action of an external field, so that the ellipsoidal shape is theequilibrium shape. This would introduce an additional variable so that, e.g., χ could become athermodynamic boundary condition. It is plausible that the theory for this scenario can be developed from an analogy between the demon’s action and an electric field.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-component fluid in a cubic simulation cell at fixed particle number N, volume V, and temperature T, supporting a spherical vapour–liquid interface (a droplet) at coexistence. Two standard approaches for extracting the surface tension from such a configuration are:

(i) the test-area method, in which one computes the derivative of the Helmholtz free energy with respect to a small area-preserving deformation of the interface, parameterised by χ, that turns the spherical droplet into an ellipsoid of revolution while keeping N, V, T fixed; and

(ii) the second-order virial (test-transformation) approach, in which the surface tension is read off from a second derivative of the free energy with respect to the same deformation parameter χ.

In both approaches the deformed (ellipsoidal) configuration is not an equilibrium state of the (N,V,T) ensemble: the equilibrium shape at fixed N, V, T is the sphere, so χ is not a natural thermodynamic variable and the corresponding free-energy derivatives lack a rigorous thermodynamic foundation.

Problem. Construct a thermodynamic and statistical-mechanical formalism that adds an extra control variable—an external-field-like coupling λ (a "demon action") conjugate to the deformation parameter χ—with the following properties:

(a) For each prescribed value of χ within some neighbourhood of the spherical shape, there exists a value of λ such that, in the extended ensemble at fixed (N, V, T, λ), the ellipsoidally deformed droplet with that χ is the true equilibrium interface shape (analogous to how an electric field selects a polarised equilibrium state of a dielectric).

(b) χ enters the formalism as a legitimate thermodynamic boundary condition, with a well-defined conjugate intensive variable λ and a free energy F(N,V,T,λ) (or equivalently F(N,V,T,χ) via Legendre transform) whose first and second derivatives with respect to χ at χ = 0 reproduce, and rigorously justify, the test-area and second-order virial expressions for the vapour–liquid surface tension.

(c) The construction is consistent with standard equilibrium statistical mechanics, e.g. by exhibiting an explicit microscopic Hamiltonian perturbation H → H − λ·X, where X is a suitable shape order parameter conjugate to χ, and by establishing the corresponding fluctuation–response relations.

Does such a formalism exist, and if so, give an explicit construction; otherwise, identify the obstruction.
artifact.status_search_result: No published resolution of this proposed external-field/"demon" formalism for distorted droplets was found. The question is posed as a forward-looking open program, and no follow-up work establishing or refuting the construction appears to be available.

status_evidence.title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension
status_evidence.snippet: Paper explicitly frames this as an open question, suggesting a demon/external-field analogy might work but is not developed.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as an open program with no constructed formalism.
